use_notes: Belavadös DOCX and ZIP files supply world lore, race families, creator-god doctrine, daily-life tone, and time conversion data.

table_role_overview.dm: The Dungeon Master describes scenes, presents consequences, controls monsters/NPCs, and decides when a roll is needed.
table_role_overview.players: Players describe what their characters attempt, roll when the DM calls for uncertainty, and roleplay the results.
core_loop: Players describe what their characters do.
DM resolves the action through narration, rules, or dice.

dice_notation.format: XdY+Z means roll X dice with Y sides and add Z.

examples.meaning: Roll one twenty-sided die and add 4.
Roll two six-sided dice, add them together, then add 3.

d20_tests.definition: A D20 Test is a d20 roll used when the result is uncertain and meaningful. It covers ability checks, saving throws, and attack rolls.
d20_tests.formula: 1d20 + relevant ability modifier + proficiency bonus if proficient + other bonuses/penalties
d20_tests.success_rule: If the total equals or exceeds the target number, the test succeeds.

advantage_and_disadvantage.advantage: Roll two d20s and use the higher result.
advantage_and_disadvantage.disadvantage: Roll two d20s and use the lower result.
advantage_and_disadvantage.both: If both apply, they cancel to a normal single d20 roll unless a feature says otherwise.

common_roll_formulas.ability_check: 1d20 + ability modifier + proficiency bonus if relevant
common_roll_formulas.skill_check: 1d20 + default or DM-chosen ability modifier + proficiency bonus if proficient in that skill
common_roll_formulas.expertise_check: 1d20 + ability modifier + double proficiency bonus if expertise applies
common_roll_formulas.saving_throw: 1d20 + ability modifier + proficiency bonus if proficient in that save
common_roll_formulas.weapon_attack: 1d20 + relevant ability modifier + proficiency bonus if proficient with the weapon
common_roll_formulas.weapon_damage: weapon damage dice + relevant ability modifier unless a rule says otherwise
common_roll_formulas.passive_check: 10 + relevant modifiers that normally apply to the check
common_roll_formulas.death_saving_throw: 1d20 with no normal ability modifier; 10 or higher succeeds, 9 or lower fails; track 3 successes or 3 failures.

combat_basics.initiative: At combat start, each participant rolls initiative. Higher results act earlier.
turn_resources: one reaction between turns when triggered
free/object interactions as allowed by DM
attack_resolution: Roll attack if the action calls for one.
On a hit, roll damage and apply effects.

spellcasting_basics.cantrips: At-will spells that do not use spell slots.
spellcasting_basics.leveled_spells: Usually require spending a spell slot of the spell level or higher.
spellcasting_basics.spell_attack_vs_save: Some spells use a spell attack roll; some force the target to make a saving throw against your spell save DC.
spellcasting_basics.concentration: A caster can normally concentrate on only one concentration spell at a time and may need Constitution saves to maintain it after taking damage.

belavados_time_conversion_source.raw_text:
Belavadös Time Conversion Guide
Earth-first table play, Belavadös-second lore time
1. The New Rule
Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, schedules, sessions, travel, and deadlines.
Use Belavadös dates second for lore, temples, festivals, legal records, journals, and immersion.
A Belavadös year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long. For table play, those 330.15 days are distributed evenly across the Earth year.
2. Clean Math
Item	Simplified value
Belavadös solar year	330.15 Belavadös solar days
Belavadös civil calendar	11 months x 30 dates = 330 named civil dates
Earth year used for play	365 days, or 366 days in leap years
Non-leap year pace	1 Earth day = 330.15 / 365 = 0.9045205 Belavadös solar days
Leap year pace	1 Earth day = 330.15 / 366 = 0.9020492 Belavadös solar days
Non-leap Belavadös civil date length	365 / 330 = 1.10606 Earth days per named civil date
Month length on Earth calendar	365 / 11 = 33.18 Earth days per Belavadös month in a non-leap year
3. Conversion Formula
daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
earthProgress = (Earth day-of-year - 1 + fractionOfEarthDay) / daysInEarthYear.
belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this for sky, moon, season, and astronomy math.
belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this for the named calendar date.
monthIndex = floor(belCivilDateProgress / 30), from 0 to 10.
dayOfMonth = floor(belCivilDateProgress % 30) + 1.
Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.
Important distinction: the Night Sky uses the astronomical year of 330.15 Belavadös days. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates. The extra 0.15 is distributed through the year as a tiny solar/clock correction, not stored as a bonus day at the end.
4. Month Cycle
#	Month	Civil dates	Theme
1	Thoryn-Rahek	1-30	aberrant life, primordial mutation, dangerous origins
2	Freysethysra	1-30	crossroads, curses, beauty, temptation, forbidden pacts
3	Nefarokir	1-30	death, spirits, memory, burial, cosmic ledgers
4	Thalunesh	1-30	dreamers, tricksters, shapeshifters, wanderers, fey mischief
5	Horundar	1-30	storms, oceans, floods, earthquakes, raw elemental force
6	Raeshkul	1-30	intellect, psionics, strategy, higher understanding
7	Asethrimir	1-30	freedom, revelry, wilderness survival, constructs, awakened machinery
8	Sokhivar	1-30	sunlight, music, prophecy, divine freedom
9	Iskazunet	1-30	beasts, instinct, fertility, shadows, curses, twilight-born peoples
10	Bastve'enlil	1-30	tides, reefs, trenches, adaptation, civilization, instinct
11	Hathruna	1-30	rebirth, rot, fungi, roots, decay cycles
5. Weekdays
For player-facing schedules, keep the live Earth weekday mapping. This keeps sessions, transit boards, deadlines, and reminders easy to read.
Earth weekday	Belavadös weekday	Function
Monday	Nebday	Standard civic day
Tuesday	Sigranday	Standard civic day
Wednesday	Ishtaday	Rest / sync day
Thursday	Marduday	Standard civic day
Friday	Enkirday	Standard civic day
Saturday	Anubaday	Standard civic day
Sunday	Valkhaday	Standard civic day
6. Night Sky Integration
Use 330.15 Belavadös days as the astronomical year because the Night Sky file identifies Belavadös at 1.00 AU with a 330.15-day orbital period.
Use 330 named civil dates for the calendar because the civil calendar is still 11 months of 30 days.
Use solar progress, not month/date progress, for moon phases, planetary positions, constellations, tides, and sky omens.
The larger moon Chandratecu-Seleneš has a 19.20 Belavadös-day orbit; the smaller moonlet Mictlindra-Nannara has a 2.02 Belavadös-day orbit. For Earth sessions, calculate their phase from belSolarDayProgress so the sky stays smooth all year.
Because the solar correction is distributed, the Star-River, wandering worlds, and paired moons never need a special frozen/end-buffer period.
7. Province Time Zones
Each province now receives a primary Earth-style UTC label and, where useful, one neighboring secondary label. Settlement-specific exports should store the exact settlement UTC by longitude. Province summaries should show only the one or two labels below.

8. Formatting Standards
General date: Earth Month Day, Year / Belavadös Month Day, Weekday.
Exact time: Earth time with UTC or local label / Belavadös clock time.
Settlement time: include the settlement UTC if it differs from the province primary UTC.
Province summary: show one or two UTC labels only, never a long chain of every border band.
Sky event: calculate from belSolarDayProgress and display Earth-first for players.
Use case	Recommended display

monster_reference_pattern: Use creature lore to understand motivation, habitat, tactics, and negotiation hooks without treating monsters as only stat blocks.
Keep quick indexes by challenge, environment, creature type, and role so encounters can be selected quickly during play.
Separate player-facing description from DM-only tactics, secrets, and stat-block mechanics.
adventure_module_pattern: Prepare an introduction, premise, safety expectations, starting hook, scene list, map/area keys, encounter notes, treasure/rewards, and aftermath.
Use scene goals instead of a fixed script: clue, obstacle, choice, consequence, and next lead.
For dungeon or site play, each area should answer: what is visible, what changes when characters interact, what danger or opportunity exists, and what exits lead onward.
For wilderness play, track route, weather, supplies, landmarks, hazards, safe rests, and rumors without forcing one correct path.
For sidequests and short sessions, limit the structure to one clear problem, two or three meaningful scenes, a decision point, and a consequence.
errata_and_updates_pattern: Keep a corrections log for rule clarifications, table rulings, changed homebrew, and source updates.
When a rule changes, record what changed, when it changed, and whether it affects existing characters.
encounter_design_pattern: Choose a dramatic purpose first: reveal, pressure, negotiation, travel complication, rescue, chase, survival, or boss confrontation.
Then choose creatures, terrain, stakes, starting distance, visibility, objectives besides damage, and retreat or surrender outcomes.
Balance is a guideline, not a promise; signal danger clearly and let player choices matter.

belavados_table_support.tone: Dark steampunk fantasy with horror, industrial decay, infrastructure, bureaucracy, and resilient humanity.
belavados_table_support.time_use: Use Earth time first for player schedules and Belavadös time second for lore records, journals, omens, and immersion.
belavados_table_support.daily_life_connection: Travel schedules, legal ledgers, transit delays, job records, supply shortages, and divine-prison infrastructure can all become adventure hooks.
belavados_table_support.beginner_support: No player needs setting mastery before play; the rules loop stays describe, decide, roll only when uncertain, narrate consequences.

table_identity.living_world_rule: Belavadös play treats travel, weather, public records, faction trust, death omens, divine industry, and ordinary work as playable systems rather than background decoration.
table_identity.new_player_goal: A player should know what their character is trying to do, what danger or social pressure is present, what rule surface is being used, and what consequence follows from success or failure.

belavados_specific_rule_surfaces.time_and_sky: Use UTC/Earth-first scheduling for table logistics and Belavadös dates, moon states, tide states, constellations, and sky notes for in-world records.
belavados_specific_rule_surfaces.alignment: Use four independent axes: altruism, lawfulness, cooperation, and honor. Scores move over time instead of locking a character into a static label.
belavados_specific_rule_surfaces.death: Death saving throws are narrative events. A drop to 0 hit points means the death design notices the character; resurrection changes the ledger rather than erasing danger.
belavados_specific_rule_surfaces.ichor: Ichor is divine bioelectrochemical power. It fuels infrastructure and weapon craft, but requires separation, cooling, purity control, and legal handling.
belavados_specific_rule_surfaces.transit: Public travel is a system of regulated portals, skyships, steamships, trains, submarines, ferries, and caravans with inspection, fare, pass, and time-board consequences.
belavados_specific_rule_surfaces.factions: Faction tier tracks trust and authority separately from class level. It can open records, legal permissions, supplies, and transit access.

principles: In most Dungeons & Dragons campaigns, death is a temporary inconvenience disguised as tragedy. Characters fall unconscious, allies rush forward with Healing Word, a potion, or Spare the Dying, and the party continues onward. Even when someone truly dies, resurrection magic often transforms death into a logistical problem rather than a spiritual horror. In Belavadös, that changes completely. Death is no longer passive. It is no longer a simple mechanic sitting quietly behind the dice. Death is an active cosmic force. It hunts. It remembers. It corrects mistakes.

In this world, the god of death maintains a design, a sequence, and a ledger that governs every living creature. Every soul has an appointed moment of death written into reality itself. Whenever someone escapes that fate through luck, prophecy, magic, intervention, or coincidence, the design fractures. The god of death responds by pursuing the survivors until balance is restored. This transforms the tone of the campaign from heroic fantasy into supernatural dread. You should stop thinking about hit points as abstract combat resources and start thinking about survival as something fragile and temporary.

To make this concept work inside Dungeons & Dragons 5e, death saving throws become narrative events instead of silent dice rolls. Every failed death save should feel like death physically reaching toward your character. Every success should feel temporary and unnatural. Rather than quietly marking successes and failures on paper, I will describe the experience in vivid sensory detail. A failed death save might feel like icy water filling your lungs, invisible hands pulling your soul downward, distant funeral bells echoing through darkness, flickering visions of graves, or whispers from unseen entities. A successful death save will not feel triumphant. It will feel stolen. Your character survives something they were never supposed to survive.

The philosophy behind unconsciousness changes as well. In standard 5e, reaching zero hit points usually means a character is bleeding out. In this setting, reaching zero hit points means the god of death has noticed your character personally. The moment you drop to zero, reality begins bending around you. Candles extinguish. Clocks stop ticking. Animals panic. Mirrors crack. Rain begins suddenly. Small environmental omens reinforce that death is not simply waiting for three failed saves. Death is already in the room.

Death saving throws themselves represent your soul resisting the claim of the death god. A success represents your soul dragging itself back into your body. A failure represents death tightening its grasp. Rolling a natural 1 becomes terrifying because your character briefly crosses into the realm of the dead and returns with fragmented memories of it. Rolling a natural 20 is deeply unsettling rather than heroic. Instead of simply regaining 1 hit point, your character violently awakens with visions of future deaths, prophetic hallucinations, or impossible knowledge they were never meant to possess.

One of the most important themes of Belavadös is inevitability. Death cannot truly be defeated. It can only be delayed, redirected, or bargained with. There are only two known ways to escape the design for any meaningful amount of time. The first is murder. By intentionally killing another person, a character steals the remaining years from the victim’s destined lifespan. The second is temporary death followed by resurrection. A character who genuinely dies and is revived becomes difficult for the death god to track because their name briefly leaves the cosmic ledger before being rewritten.

The murder mechanic is intentionally mysterious. I will never reduce it to a visible countdown or numerical timer. Stolen years function more like metaphysical momentum. A murderer becomes harder for death to claim because another life has been substituted into the design. The victim effectively takes the killer’s place in the sequence. This creates horrifying moral tension throughout the campaign. Good aligned characters may be forced to confront the possibility that survival requires evil. Cowards may become killers. Noble characters may choose sacrifice instead of stealing innocent years. Some may rationalize murdering criminals, tyrants, or dying enemies. Others may spiral into paranoia and predation.

Mechanically, I may track this through something called borrowed years. Whenever a character intentionally kills an intelligent creature as part of a conscious attempt to escape death, I secretly determine how much protection was gained based on the victim’s remaining lifespan and importance within the design. During this protected period, death cannot directly target that character through supernatural accidents or unavoidable omens. However, the psychological burden grows heavier.

Characters carrying stolen years begin deteriorating emotionally and spiritually. They suffer recurring dreams from the victim’s perspective. They hear the dead person’s voice in crowded rooms. Their reflection occasionally resembles the victim. Animals react with fear or aggression around them. Clerics sense spiritual contamination. Resurrection magic cast upon them may behave unpredictably. This ensures that murder never becomes a clean optimization strategy. Extending life through violence leaves visible scars on the soul.

The second survival method, dying and being revived, preserves hope without removing fear. In this setting, resurrection magic does not defeat death. It only confuses the design temporarily. When a creature dies and returns to life, the death god loses track of the soul for a limited time because the soul crossed the boundary correctly before returning. This creates an important distinction between ordinary healing and true resurrection.

Healing magic does not protect against the design. Healing Word, Cure Wounds, and potions restore the body, but they do not erase the fact that the soul was marked for collection. Revivify, Raise Dead, Resurrection, and similar spells genuinely interrupt the cosmic sequence. Low level healing is no longer enough to escape consequences. Survival requires confronting death directly.

Revivify becomes especially significant because it resembles magical resuscitation. The character truly dies for a brief moment before returning. During that instant, they glimpse the realm of the death god. Every revived character returns changed. Perhaps their body temperature remains unnaturally cold forever. Perhaps mirrors stop reflecting them properly. Maybe food tastes like ash. Maybe they hear whispers whenever they are alone. Resurrection leaves permanent marks.

I may represent these through marks of return. Every resurrection leaves behind a supernatural alteration chosen to reinforce the horror and atmosphere of the setting. One character may lose the ability to sleep naturally. Another may bleed black instead of red. Another might attract ghosts. Another may permanently smell faintly of grave dirt after rainfall. These changes are not meant to heavily punish players mechanically. Their purpose is narrative dread and immersion.

Death itself behaves intelligently and creatively. The environment becomes hostile in subtle escalating ways. At first, accidents seem coincidental. A chandelier sways overhead. A horse panics unexpectedly. Oil spills across stone floors. A bridge creaks ominously. Over time, the pattern becomes undeniable. Reality itself is attempting to complete the design.

These sequences are never meant to feel unfair. The horror comes from inevitability and tension rather than arbitrary punishment. There will always be clues beforehand and opportunities to intervene. A tavern fire begins with smoke, nervous servants, and crackling beams long before collapse occurs. A wagon accident begins with frightened horses and damaged wheels. You will recognize danger approaching even if you cannot fully predict how events will unfold.
table_procedures: Describe each death saving throw as a visible and sensory omen.
Treat successful death saves as temporary resistance, not triumph.
Treat failed death saves as death tightening its claim.
Use resurrection as ledger disruption with permanent marks of return.
Keep stolen-years mechanics mysterious; never turn them into a clean optimization counter.

paragraphs: A complete guide for players and Dungeon Masters
By William Saville, also known as The Transgender T-Rex #TheTransgenderTRex

I built this system to make alignment feel alive instead of frozen. Belavadös treats morality as a profile instead of a label, so characters can grow, slide, fail, recover, and surprise the table in a way that still stays easy to read.

This guide is written for Dungeon Masters, veteran D&D; players who know the old alignment grid, and new players who need a clean way in. I keep the language direct, the rules visible, and the moving parts organized so the system can be learned without losing its depth.
Nothing here is meant to trap a character in a box. Your choices shape your path, and your path reshapes your destiny.
How I want you to use this guide

For DMs, the recommendation is to start with the core axes, then move into the phase rules, and finally the XP sections. These pages establish how to run the system consistently and fairly at the table. For veteran players, the conversion material translates the old two-axis model into the newer four-axis profile system, preserving familiar ideas while adding precision and reducing ambiguity around labels. For new players, the first half of the guide is sufficient to begin play—focus on the axes, review the examples, and understand the difference between fit awards and shift awards. The appendices function as reference material you can consult when needed during play.
What I built this system to do

The system is designed to measure selfishness, lawfulness, cooperation, and honor as separate and independent questions rather than collapsing them into a single alignment label. This allows a character to be lawful yet selfish, cooperative yet dishonorable, or honorable while actively rejecting institutions. The result is a clearer moral shape that is easier to understand and roleplay.

It also emphasizes long-term behavioral patterns over isolated actions. A single act of kindness does not elevate a character into sainthood, just as a single cruel decision does not erase a lifetime of decency. Instead, Belavadös tracks patterns, turning points, sacrifices, betrayals, and repeated behavior to build a more stable and meaningful moral profile.
Quick Roadmap
Audience Guidance
What I built and why it is different

Belavadös treats morality as a living profile rather than a single alignment label. Instead of compressing ethical identity into a fixed nine-box system like traditional D&D alignment, it evaluates a character through four independent axes. Each axis measures a different moral or behavioral pressure, allowing for more nuance and less forced categorization.
Belavadös Moral Axes

This separation is important because real characters rarely fit cleanly into a single moral box. A selfish mercenary is not the same as a dishonorable traitor. A lawful bureaucrat is not automatically cooperative. A cooperative rebel is not necessarily altruistic, and an honorable outlaw may still reject institutional authority entirely. By keeping these axes distinct, Belavadös preserves moral complexity instead of flattening it into broad labels.

The system is also designed to reflect change over time. Each axis can shift as a character grows, deteriorates, or reacts to events. This turns morality into a dynamic record rather than a static label—allowing the system to track a character’s moral biography as they develop, rather than assigning them a single permanent identity.
The four alignment axes
Every character in Belavadös is measured across four independent moral dimensions. Each axis runs from 0 to 3000 points, and 1500 is the neutral center.
If you only remember one thing from this page, remember this: the axes are separate. A character can be high on one axis and low on another without contradiction. That is the heart of the system.
Alignment phases, position steps, and crossing boundaries

I divide every axis into three phases. The low phase, the neutral phase, and the high phase each contain four tracked | positions on the character sheet. That gives me a simple, readable way to show not only where a character stands, | but how far they have moved.
Here are your contents organized into clear tables:
Phase Ranges
Phase Tracking Positions
Point Change System

When a character reaches the edge of a phase, they step into the next phase at the correct corresponding position. A | change of 250 points moves the character one position. Larger changes can leap several positions at once when a | major event deserves it.
Character creation and starting scores

At character creation, or through birth, adoption, awakening, or transformation in game, I let players start in more than | one way. They may take a short scenario based alignment test, choose their alignment manually, or build from a | background, oath, faction, or backstory that clearly points in a direction.

The default starting point for every axis is 1500. That means a new character begins at the neutral center unless the | fiction says otherwise. A DM may shift starting scores by about 100 to 300 points for an ordinary background, and by | larger amounts when divine influence, faction indoctrination, or a very strong concept justifies it.
Strong concept or divine influence Larger shifts are allowed when the fiction justifies it.

I use those modifiers to create distinct personalities without permanently locking anyone into a rigid moral box. The goal is to give the character a believable starting shape, then let play do the rest.
Alignment is dynamic
Your actions continuously shape your moral trajectory. I do not treat alignment as something a player gets stuck with forever. I treat it as something that evolves through play.
A character can begin in one place and end up somewhere very different after one meaningful betrayal, sacrifice, or turning point. That is not a bug in the system. That is the point of it.

In play, I usually think in patterns. One kind act matters, but a repeated pattern of sacrifice matters more. One cruel | choice matters, but a repeated habit of exploitation matters more. The score should reflect the true story of the | character, not a single scene taken in isolation.
Why alignment matters at the table
Belavadös is not just a label system. It is a living reputation system. When the table uses it well, the world can answer the characters in different ways depending on how they have actually behaved.

That means the system can influence trust, fear, admiration, hostility, political standing, access to sacred spaces, rare dialogue, faction invitations, and the kind of legacy people speak about after the session ends.
I want the world to react to the character in distinct ways, not just say they are good or evil. That is why I separate honor from lawfulness and cooperation from altruism.
Running Belavadös in D&D; 5e

Belavadös replaces the rigid old grid with four continuous behavioral axes. That makes it easier to model gradual | change, mixed motives, and morally complicated characters while still staying fully compatible with D&D; 5e roleplay, | factions, magic items, subclasses, divine systems, and reputation mechanics.
When you need to translate old alignment language, I treat it as a threshold question rather than a binary label. Here’s your content organized into a clear table format:
Moral & Behavioral Trait Definitions
Design Interpretation (Belavadös System)
This is still D&D; at the table. I am not replacing the game. I am giving the table a finer tool for reading character identity and narrative consequence.
Rewarding alignment play

I use the same reward logic for both advancement modes. The difference is not what gets rewarded. The difference is | when the points are handed out. My rule of thumb is simple. If a choice is merely on brand, it gets a fit award. If it | genuinely changes the character's direction, it gets a shift award.

A small repeatable behavior should not create a massive shift by itself. A meaningful scene choice should matter. A major moral decision should matter a lot. A campaign defining sacrifice, betrayal, or oath should matter even more.
I also keep the table honest by tying rewards to visible narrative consequences, not to table noise or repetitive point | farming.
Adventuring XP mode
Adventuring XP is the granular version. I use it when the table likes seeing immediate progress and wants alignment to feel like part of the normal rhythm of play.

I award points at the end of each notable scene. I only award for choices with risk, cost, or public consequence. I do | not award for filler talk, repeated probing, or harmless chatter. The system should reward meaningful roleplay, not | table noise.

When a choice fits the current profile, I count that as a fit award. When the choice changes the profile in a way that matters later, I count that as a shift award. A single scene can earn both, but only when both parts are true.
Milestone XP mode
Milestone XP is the chapter based version. I use it when the campaign is narrative heavy, the table is open ended, or the group wants less bookkeeping during a session.

Milestone mode solves the bookkeeping problem without changing the reward logic. I still reward the same kinds of alignment moments, but I log them during play and hand them out at the end of the session, chapter, or story beat.
That keeps the table moving while still making the alignment system feel alive and responsive.
Axis triggers
These triggers are the practical heart of the system. When I look at a scene, I ask which axis the choice touches and whether the action is pushing the character up or down that axis.
5e compatible examples
I keep these examples simple on purpose. They give the DM a clean starting point, but they are not hard limits. The fiction matters more than the exact spell name or combat move.

If an action has both mechanical and narrative weight, I lean into the narrative weight first. Saving an ally in a life or | death moment is not the same thing as casually helping with a small task. The difference should be visible in the | reward.
Translating items, abilities, and world reactions
When old 5e content references alignment, I translate it into thresholds instead of binary labels. That lets me keep the spirit of the item or effect while making the requirement fit the new system.
Traditional requirement | Belavadös translation
A clean DM rule and the veteran player conversion guide

I use alignment as a living reputation system, not a punishment system. I award points only when actions meaningfully | impact story, relationships, faction standing, moral consequences, or character identity. I avoid rewarding repetitive | behavior farming.
For veteran players, the old two axis model still helps as a memory aid. I just split the old idea into four questions so it becomes easier to read mixed characters.

A traditional lawful good hero will usually read as lawful, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. A chaotic good hero | will usually read as lawless, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. A character that was simply neutral in the old model | can land in many different places here, because neutral in the old system often meant the label was not trying to | describe that axis very strongly.
New player quick start and DM guardrails
For new players, the easiest way to use this system is to play your character honestly, say why they are acting when the choice matters, and ask me which axis a decision touches if you are unsure.
If two players make the same choice for different reasons, the motive can matter. Keep the table consistent and explain the rule before the campaign starts.

My fairness rule is simple. If the table can explain the award in one sentence, the award is probably clear enough. If it takes five sentences, I log the moment and settle it at the end of the session.
I do not punish imperfect roleplay. I reward intention and consequence. The goal is to help players explore the system, not to turn the table into a test they can fail by accident.
Optional rules and a session tracker
These rules keep the system tight when the campaign needs more control. They are optional, but I use them often when I want cleaner pacing and less argument.
Example Session Tracker
Example starting spreads and archetypes
These starting spreads help me seed characters with a clear moral shape without locking them into a final identity. They are examples, not cages.

sections.heading: A complete guide for players and Dungeon Masters
By William Saville, also known as The Transgender T-Rex #TheTransgenderTRex
content: I built this system to make alignment feel alive instead of frozen. Belavadös treats morality as a profile instead of a label, so characters can grow, slide, fail, recover, and surprise the table in a way that still stays easy to read.

This guide is written for Dungeon Masters, veteran D&D; players who know the old alignment grid, and new players who need a clean way in. I keep the language direct, the rules visible, and the moving parts organized so the system can be learned without losing its depth.
Nothing here is meant to trap a character in a box. Your choices shape your path, and your path reshapes your destiny.

sections.heading: How I want you to use this guide
content: For DMs, the recommendation is to start with the core axes, then move into the phase rules, and finally the XP sections. These pages establish how to run the system consistently and fairly at the table. For veteran players, the conversion material translates the old two-axis model into the newer four-axis profile system, preserving familiar ideas while adding precision and reducing ambiguity around labels. For new players, the first half of the guide is sufficient to begin play—focus on the axes, review the examples, and understand the difference between fit awards and shift awards. The appendices function as reference material you can consult when needed during play.

sections.heading: What I built this system to do
content: The system is designed to measure selfishness, lawfulness, cooperation, and honor as separate and independent questions rather than collapsing them into a single alignment label. This allows a character to be lawful yet selfish, cooperative yet dishonorable, or honorable while actively rejecting institutions. The result is a clearer moral shape that is easier to understand and roleplay.

It also emphasizes long-term behavioral patterns over isolated actions. A single act of kindness does not elevate a character into sainthood, just as a single cruel decision does not erase a lifetime of decency. Instead, Belavadös tracks patterns, turning points, sacrifices, betrayals, and repeated behavior to build a more stable and meaningful moral profile.

sections.heading: What I built and why it is different
content: Belavadös treats morality as a living profile rather than a single alignment label. Instead of compressing ethical identity into a fixed nine-box system like traditional D&D alignment, it evaluates a character through four independent axes. Each axis measures a different moral or behavioral pressure, allowing for more nuance and less forced categorization.

sections.heading: Belavadös Moral Axes
content: This separation is important because real characters rarely fit cleanly into a single moral box. A selfish mercenary is not the same as a dishonorable traitor. A lawful bureaucrat is not automatically cooperative. A cooperative rebel is not necessarily altruistic, and an honorable outlaw may still reject institutional authority entirely. By keeping these axes distinct, Belavadös preserves moral complexity instead of flattening it into broad labels.

The system is also designed to reflect change over time. Each axis can shift as a character grows, deteriorates, or reacts to events. This turns morality into a dynamic record rather than a static label—allowing the system to track a character’s moral biography as they develop, rather than assigning them a single permanent identity.

sections.heading: The four alignment axes
content: Every character in Belavadös is measured across four independent moral dimensions. Each axis runs from 0 to 3000 points, and 1500 is the neutral center.
If you only remember one thing from this page, remember this: the axes are separate. A character can be high on one axis and low on another without contradiction. That is the heart of the system.

sections.heading: Alignment phases, position steps, and crossing boundaries
content: I divide every axis into three phases. The low phase, the neutral phase, and the high phase each contain four tracked | positions on the character sheet. That gives me a simple, readable way to show not only where a character stands, | but how far they have moved.
Here are your contents organized into clear tables:

sections.heading: Point Change System
content: When a character reaches the edge of a phase, they step into the next phase at the correct corresponding position. A | change of 250 points moves the character one position. Larger changes can leap several positions at once when a | major event deserves it.

sections.heading: Character creation and starting scores
content: At character creation, or through birth, adoption, awakening, or transformation in game, I let players start in more than | one way. They may take a short scenario based alignment test, choose their alignment manually, or build from a | background, oath, faction, or backstory that clearly points in a direction.

The default starting point for every axis is 1500. That means a new character begins at the neutral center unless the | fiction says otherwise. A DM may shift starting scores by about 100 to 300 points for an ordinary background, and by | larger amounts when divine influence, faction indoctrination, or a very strong concept justifies it.
Strong concept or divine influence Larger shifts are allowed when the fiction justifies it.

I use those modifiers to create distinct personalities without permanently locking anyone into a rigid moral box. The goal is to give the character a believable starting shape, then let play do the rest.

sections.heading: Alignment is dynamic
content: Your actions continuously shape your moral trajectory. I do not treat alignment as something a player gets stuck with forever. I treat it as something that evolves through play.
A character can begin in one place and end up somewhere very different after one meaningful betrayal, sacrifice, or turning point. That is not a bug in the system. That is the point of it.

In play, I usually think in patterns. One kind act matters, but a repeated pattern of sacrifice matters more. One cruel | choice matters, but a repeated habit of exploitation matters more. The score should reflect the true story of the | character, not a single scene taken in isolation.

sections.heading: Why alignment matters at the table
content: Belavadös is not just a label system. It is a living reputation system. When the table uses it well, the world can answer the characters in different ways depending on how they have actually behaved.

That means the system can influence trust, fear, admiration, hostility, political standing, access to sacred spaces, rare dialogue, faction invitations, and the kind of legacy people speak about after the session ends.
I want the world to react to the character in distinct ways, not just say they are good or evil. That is why I separate honor from lawfulness and cooperation from altruism.

sections.heading: Running Belavadös in D&D; 5e
content: Belavadös replaces the rigid old grid with four continuous behavioral axes. That makes it easier to model gradual | change, mixed motives, and morally complicated characters while still staying fully compatible with D&D; 5e roleplay, | factions, magic items, subclasses, divine systems, and reputation mechanics.
When you need to translate old alignment language, I treat it as a threshold question rather than a binary label. Here’s your content organized into a clear table format:

sections.heading: Design Interpretation (Belavadös System)
content: This is still D&D; at the table. I am not replacing the game. I am giving the table a finer tool for reading character identity and narrative consequence.

sections.heading: Rewarding alignment play
content: I use the same reward logic for both advancement modes. The difference is not what gets rewarded. The difference is | when the points are handed out. My rule of thumb is simple. If a choice is merely on brand, it gets a fit award. If it | genuinely changes the character's direction, it gets a shift award.

A small repeatable behavior should not create a massive shift by itself. A meaningful scene choice should matter. A major moral decision should matter a lot. A campaign defining sacrifice, betrayal, or oath should matter even more.
I also keep the table honest by tying rewards to visible narrative consequences, not to table noise or repetitive point | farming.

sections.heading: Adventuring XP mode
content: Adventuring XP is the granular version. I use it when the table likes seeing immediate progress and wants alignment to feel like part of the normal rhythm of play.

I award points at the end of each notable scene. I only award for choices with risk, cost, or public consequence. I do | not award for filler talk, repeated probing, or harmless chatter. The system should reward meaningful roleplay, not | table noise.

When a choice fits the current profile, I count that as a fit award. When the choice changes the profile in a way that matters later, I count that as a shift award. A single scene can earn both, but only when both parts are true.

sections.heading: Milestone XP mode
content: Milestone XP is the chapter based version. I use it when the campaign is narrative heavy, the table is open ended, or the group wants less bookkeeping during a session.

Milestone mode solves the bookkeeping problem without changing the reward logic. I still reward the same kinds of alignment moments, but I log them during play and hand them out at the end of the session, chapter, or story beat.
That keeps the table moving while still making the alignment system feel alive and responsive.

sections.heading: Axis triggers
content: These triggers are the practical heart of the system. When I look at a scene, I ask which axis the choice touches and whether the action is pushing the character up or down that axis.

sections.heading: 5e compatible examples
content: I keep these examples simple on purpose. They give the DM a clean starting point, but they are not hard limits. The fiction matters more than the exact spell name or combat move.

If an action has both mechanical and narrative weight, I lean into the narrative weight first. Saving an ally in a life or | death moment is not the same thing as casually helping with a small task. The difference should be visible in the | reward.

sections.heading: Translating items, abilities, and world reactions
content: When old 5e content references alignment, I translate it into thresholds instead of binary labels. That lets me keep the spirit of the item or effect while making the requirement fit the new system.

sections.heading: A clean DM rule and the veteran player conversion guide
content: I use alignment as a living reputation system, not a punishment system. I award points only when actions meaningfully | impact story, relationships, faction standing, moral consequences, or character identity. I avoid rewarding repetitive | behavior farming.
For veteran players, the old two axis model still helps as a memory aid. I just split the old idea into four questions so it becomes easier to read mixed characters.

A traditional lawful good hero will usually read as lawful, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. A chaotic good hero | will usually read as lawless, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. sections.heading: Final philosophy
content: Belavadös is not about assigning permanent labels. It is about consequences, reputation, ideology, personal evolution, social perception, and moral complexity.

paragraphs: The Design of Death in Belavadös

In most Dungeons & Dragons campaigns, death is a temporary inconvenience disguised as tragedy. Characters fall unconscious, allies rush forward with Healing Word, a potion, or Spare the Dying, and the party continues onward. Even when someone truly dies, resurrection magic often transforms death into a logistical problem rather than a spiritual horror. In Belavadös, that changes completely. Death is no longer passive. It is no longer a simple mechanic sitting quietly behind the dice. Death is an active cosmic force. It hunts. It remembers. It corrects mistakes.

In this world, the god of death maintains a design, a sequence, and a ledger that governs every living creature. Every soul has an appointed moment of death written into reality itself. Whenever someone escapes that fate through luck, prophecy, magic, intervention, or coincidence, the design fractures. The god of death responds by pursuing the survivors until balance is restored. This transforms the tone of the campaign from heroic fantasy into supernatural dread. You should stop thinking about hit points as abstract combat resources and start thinking about survival as something fragile and temporary.

To make this concept work inside Dungeons & Dragons 5e, death saving throws become narrative events instead of silent dice rolls. Every failed death save should feel like death physically reaching toward your character. Every success should feel temporary and unnatural. Rather than quietly marking successes and failures on paper, I will describe the experience in vivid sensory detail. A failed death save might feel like icy water filling your lungs, invisible hands pulling your soul downward, distant funeral bells echoing through darkness, flickering visions of graves, or whispers from unseen entities. A successful death save will not feel triumphant. It will feel stolen. Your character survives something they were never supposed to survive.

The philosophy behind unconsciousness changes as well. In standard 5e, reaching zero hit points usually means a character is bleeding out. In this setting, reaching zero hit points means the god of death has noticed your character personally. The moment you drop to zero, reality begins bending around you. Candles extinguish. Clocks stop ticking. Animals panic. Mirrors crack. Rain begins suddenly. Small environmental omens reinforce that death is not simply waiting for three failed saves. Death is already in the room.

Death saving throws themselves represent your soul resisting the claim of the death god. A success represents your soul dragging itself back into your body. A failure represents death tightening its grasp. Rolling a natural 1 becomes terrifying because your character briefly crosses into the realm of the dead and returns with fragmented memories of it. Rolling a natural 20 is deeply unsettling rather than heroic. Instead of simply regaining 1 hit point, your character violently awakens with visions of future deaths, prophetic hallucinations, or impossible knowledge they were never meant to possess.

One of the most important themes of Belavadös is inevitability. Death cannot truly be defeated. It can only be delayed, redirected, or bargained with. There are only two known ways to escape the design for any meaningful amount of time. The first is murder. By intentionally killing another person, a character steals the remaining years from the victim’s destined lifespan. The second is temporary death followed by resurrection. A character who genuinely dies and is revived becomes difficult for the death god to track because their name briefly leaves the cosmic ledger before being rewritten.

The murder mechanic is intentionally mysterious. I will never reduce it to a visible countdown or numerical timer. Stolen years function more like metaphysical momentum. A murderer becomes harder for death to claim because another life has been substituted into the design. The victim effectively takes the killer’s place in the sequence. This creates horrifying moral tension throughout the campaign. Good aligned characters may be forced to confront the possibility that survival requires evil. Cowards may become killers. Noble characters may choose sacrifice instead of stealing innocent years. Some may rationalize murdering criminals, tyrants, or dying enemies. Others may spiral into paranoia and predation.

Mechanically, I may track this through something called borrowed years. Whenever a character intentionally kills an intelligent creature as part of a conscious attempt to escape death, I secretly determine how much protection was gained based on the victim’s remaining lifespan and importance within the design. During this protected period, death cannot directly target that character through supernatural accidents or unavoidable omens. However, the psychological burden grows heavier.

Characters carrying stolen years begin deteriorating emotionally and spiritually. They suffer recurring dreams from the victim’s perspective. They hear the dead person’s voice in crowded rooms. Their reflection occasionally resembles the victim. Animals react with fear or aggression around them. Clerics sense spiritual contamination. Resurrection magic cast upon them may behave unpredictably. This ensures that murder never becomes a clean optimization strategy. Extending life through violence leaves visible scars on the soul.

The second survival method, dying and being revived, preserves hope without removing fear. In this setting, resurrection magic does not defeat death. It only confuses the design temporarily. When a creature dies and returns to life, the death god loses track of the soul for a limited time because the soul crossed the boundary correctly before returning. This creates an important distinction between ordinary healing and true resurrection.

Healing magic does not protect against the design. Healing Word, Cure Wounds, and potions restore the body, but they do not erase the fact that the soul was marked for collection. Revivify, Raise Dead, Resurrection, and similar spells genuinely interrupt the cosmic sequence. Low level healing is no longer enough to escape consequences. Survival requires confronting death directly.

Revivify becomes especially significant because it resembles magical resuscitation. The character truly dies for a brief moment before returning. During that instant, they glimpse the realm of the death god. Every revived character returns changed. Perhaps their body temperature remains unnaturally cold forever. Perhaps mirrors stop reflecting them properly. Maybe food tastes like ash. Maybe they hear whispers whenever they are alone. Resurrection leaves permanent marks.

I may represent these through marks of return. Every resurrection leaves behind a supernatural alteration chosen to reinforce the horror and atmosphere of the setting. One character may lose the ability to sleep naturally. Another may bleed black instead of red. Another might attract ghosts. Another may permanently smell faintly of grave dirt after rainfall. These changes are not meant to heavily punish players mechanically. Their purpose is narrative dread and immersion.

Death itself behaves intelligently and creatively. The environment becomes hostile in subtle escalating ways. At first, accidents seem coincidental. A chandelier sways overhead. A horse panics unexpectedly. Oil spills across stone floors. A bridge creaks ominously. Over time, the pattern becomes undeniable. Reality itself is attempting to complete the design.

These sequences are never meant to feel unfair. The horror comes from inevitability and tension rather than arbitrary punishment. There will always be clues beforehand and opportunities to intervene. A tavern fire begins with smoke, nervous servants, and crackling beams long before collapse occurs. A wagon accident begins with frightened horses and damaged wheels. You will recognize danger approaching even if you cannot fully predict how events will unfold.

Environmental hazards are layered together deliberately. A leaking lantern alone is not frightening. A leaking lantern beside spilled alcohol near frightened horses during a thunderstorm while an exhausted blacksmith works nearby becomes terrifying. You should begin examining your surroundings constantly. Ordinary environments become sources of paranoia.

Combat changes dramatically under this system as well. Battles stop being isolated tactical encounters and instead become opportunities for death itself to interfere. A fighter reduced to zero hit points may suddenly notice the battlefield turning against them. Broken pillars collapse. Loose arrows ignite spilled oil. A dying enemy accidentally triggers a trap. The god of death manipulates probability itself.

Resurrection magic across the world carries a darker reputation. Priests no longer treat resurrection casually. Temples fear repeated revivals because they attract the attention of the death god. Clerics understand that every resurrection creates imbalance. Some faiths outlaw resurrection entirely except under extreme circumstances. Others demand terrible sacrifices in exchange.

Diamonds used for resurrection magic become symbolically important in this setting. They may be crystallized fragments of souls that resisted death long ago. Each resurrection literally burns spiritual essence to obscure a soul from the design temporarily. Material spell components stop feeling transactional and begin carrying thematic weight.

NPCs who escaped death become deeply unsettling figures throughout the campaign. You may encounter a man who murdered dozens to extend his lifespan yet still sees death approaching everywhere. You may meet an old queen resurrected six times whose body slowly decays despite remaining alive. You may discover assassins hired specifically to kill marked individuals before the design escalates into larger catastrophes.

Visions are another major roleplaying element. Characters marked by death occasionally receive prophetic glimpses of future fatalities. These visions are fragmented, symbolic, and incomplete. A character may see shattered stained glass, hear children screaming, and smell smoke days before a cathedral collapse. Another may glimpse blood floating in bathwater before a noble’s murder. These visions create tension because disaster is coming even when its meaning remains unclear.

The order of death also matters. After surviving a catastrophe, characters may realize the design is pursuing them in sequence. Each death changes who is next. Every resurrection, sacrifice, and murder reshapes the order. The party may begin obsessively tracking the sequence themselves. Entire sessions may revolve around preventing disasters before they occur.

This naturally encourages strong roleplay because every character reacts differently to mortality. One may become recklessly nihilistic. Another may become deeply religious. Another may pursue immortality through forbidden magic. Another may emotionally isolate themselves to avoid hurting others when death eventually arrives.
At the center of the campaign lies one question. What are people willing to do to survive?

That question becomes even more disturbing when innocent people become endangered by the design. If death cannot reach its target directly, collateral damage escalates. Buildings collapse. Ships sink. Fires spread through crowded districts. The party gradually realizes their continued survival threatens everyone around them.

This creates opportunities for moral horror. A character protected by stolen years may remain temporarily safe while everyone nearby suffers escalating danger. Communities may fear those who have been resurrected. Entire towns may exile marked individuals. Some groups may argue that one person should willingly die to stop the cycle.

Exhaustion and trauma may reinforce the emotional cost of cheating death. Repeated resurrections strain the spirit. Repeated survival leaves psychological scars. Characters may become sleepless, detached, paranoid, or emotionally numb from constantly standing at the edge of mortality.

Death omens appear more frequently around marked characters. Ravens gather nearby. Milk spoils instantly. Insects swarm unnaturally. Strangers avoid eye contact without understanding why. Divination magic becomes distorted in subtle ways.

The death god itself remains mostly unseen. The less directly understood it is, the more frightening it becomes. It is not a traditional villain giving speeches or issuing threats. It behaves more like a cosmic law with intelligence behind it. It does not hate mortals. It simply restores balance.

Occasionally, however, its agents may appear. Pale masked figures, grave wardens, psychopomps, or silent observers may arrive near disasters or resurrection sites. Sometimes they simply watch. Sometimes they warn against further resistance. Sometimes they quietly collect souls after tragedy strikes.

Death is also patient. If the party successfully avoids one attempt, the pressure may vanish temporarily. Life appears normal again. Tension fades. Weeks later, another elaborate chain of events begins unexpectedly. This unpredictability keeps the atmosphere from becoming repetitive.

The structure of the campaign supports investigation based storytelling beautifully. The party may uncover records of previous death cycles. Entire villages may have vanished centuries ago after someone cheated death repeatedly. Ancient kings may have massacred thousands to extend their reigns. Hidden cults may worship the death god by helping restore the proper order.

Even undead creatures fit naturally into this cosmology. Ghosts are souls that escaped collection improperly. Revenants are beings intentionally allowed to persist until an imbalance is corrected. Liches represent ultimate rebellion against the design. Vampires survive by stealing life essence because they permanently exist outside the natural cycle.

The atmosphere of the campaign constantly emphasizes fragility. I will describe unstable architecture, old ropes, cracked glass, slippery stones, flickering flames, rusted chains, and exhausted workers with deliberate detail. Ordinary objects become threatening because the environment itself can become part of the design.

At the same time, moments of humanity become even more important. Quiet campfire conversations matter because survival is uncertain. Friendships deepen because nobody expects longevity. Romance becomes tragic because every future feels fragile.

Survivor’s guilt becomes unavoidable for many characters. Anyone who escapes through murder or resurrection eventually questions whether they deserved to survive. Clerics may struggle with their faith after reviving companions repeatedly. Paladins may break their oaths. Rogues may rationalize atrocities. Even successful survival leaves emotional consequences.

Prophecy also becomes deeply unsettling. Seers and oracles are feared because they glimpse fragments of the design constantly. Some blind themselves to avoid seeing death everywhere they look. Others profit by selling incomplete warnings. False prophecies become especially dangerous because misunderstanding the design often accelerates disaster instead of preventing it.

During major death sequences, pacing changes dramatically. Narration slows. Positioning matters. Every sound and movement becomes important. A simple tavern scene can become terrifying once every object in the room suddenly feels dangerous.

Mechanically, I want to avoid overcomplicating the system. The power of Belavadös comes primarily from atmosphere, roleplay, and tension. Standard 5e mechanics already support much of this naturally. Only minor adjustments are necessary.

One possible adjustment is preventing failed death saves from resetting immediately through ordinary healing. In standard 5e, any healing clears failed saves completely. In Belavadös, failed saves may linger until a long rest because your soul was still touched by death. This makes repeated knockdowns increasingly dangerous.

I may also track a hidden pressure system for each character. Escaping fatal events, surviving prophecies, using resurrection magic, or stealing years increases the pressure surrounding that character. The higher it grows, the more aggressively reality attempts correction. You will never know the exact number, only the escalating consequences.

Most importantly, Belavadös depends on everyone embracing the tone together. Death is omnipresent, psychologically oppressive, and morally corrosive. Survival always carries a cost. Fear, tension, investigation, and character drama are central to the experience.
Every combat becomes meaningful. Every resurrection becomes emotionally significant. Every death save becomes terrifying.

By treating death as an intelligent cosmic force instead of a simple mechanical state, the campaign transforms into something uniquely haunting. The question eventually stops being whether your characters can survive. The real question becomes what survival is worth.
In the end, the true horror of this setting is not dying. The true horror is discovering what people become when death refuses to let them go.

Hidden cults may worship the death god by helping restore the proper order.

Even undead creatures fit naturally into this cosmology. Ghosts are souls that escaped collection improperly. Revenants are beings intentionally allowed to persist until an imbalance is corrected. Liches represent ultimate rebellion against the design. Vampires survive by stealing life essence because they permanently exist outside the natural cycle.

The atmosphere of the campaign constantly emphasizes fragility. I will describe unstable architecture, old ropes, cracked glass, slippery stones, flickering flames, rusted chains, and exhausted workers with deliberate detail. Ordinary objects become threatening because the environment itself can become part of the design.

At the same time, moments of humanity become even more important. Quiet campfire conversations matter because survival is uncertain. Friendships deepen because nobody expects longevity. Romance becomes tragic because every future feels fragile.

Survivor’s guilt becomes unavoidable for many characters. Anyone who escapes through murder or resurrection eventually questions whether they deserved to survive. Clerics may struggle with their faith after reviving companions repeatedly. Paladins may break their oaths. Rogues may rationalize atrocities. Even successful survival leaves emotional consequences.

Prophecy also becomes deeply unsettling. Seers and oracles are feared because they glimpse fragments of the design constantly. Some blind themselves to avoid seeing death everywhere they look. Others profit by selling incomplete warnings. False prophecies become especially dangerous because misunderstanding the design often accelerates disaster instead of preventing it.

During major death sequences, pacing changes dramatically. Narration slows. Positioning matters. Every sound and movement becomes important. A simple tavern scene can become terrifying once every object in the room suddenly feels dangerous.

Mechanically, I want to avoid overcomplicating the system. The power of Belavadös comes primarily from atmosphere, roleplay, and tension. Standard 5e mechanics already support much of this naturally. Only minor adjustments are necessary.

One possible adjustment is preventing failed death saves from resetting immediately through ordinary healing. In standard 5e, any healing clears failed saves completely. In Belavadös, failed saves may linger until a long rest because your soul was still touched by death. This makes repeated knockdowns increasingly dangerous.

I may also track a hidden pressure system for each character. Escaping fatal events, surviving prophecies, using resurrection magic, or stealing years increases the pressure surrounding that character. The higher it grows, the more aggressively reality attempts correction. You will never know the exact number, only the escalating consequences.

Most importantly, Belavadös depends on everyone embracing the tone together. Death is omnipresent, psychologically oppressive, and morally corrosive. Survival always carries a cost. Fear, tension, investigation, and character drama are central to the experience.
Every combat becomes meaningful. Every resurrection becomes emotionally significant. Every death save becomes terrifying.

By treating death as an intelligent cosmic force instead of a simple mechanical state, the campaign transforms into something uniquely haunting. The question eventually stops being whether your characters can survive. The real question becomes what survival is worth.
In the end, the true horror of this setting is not dying. The true horror is discovering what people become when death refuses to let them go.

paragraphs: Belavadös
A Long-Term Dungeons & Dragons 5th Edition Campaign

Belavadös is a long-term Dungeons & Dragons 5th Edition campaign set in a dark steampunk fantasy world shaped by industrial expansion, ancient horror, political infrastructure, and fragile systems struggling to hold civilization together. Recruitment is now open for both new and experienced players interested in collaborative storytelling, immersive worldbuilding, and a setting designed for long-term play.

This campaign is being built as a living world rather than a fixed storyline. The setting continues to grow through new regions, factions, discoveries, conflicts, and player decisions. Early recruitment is intentional so that the community, stories, and world can develop together over time. The campaign is designed to support long-running continuity while remaining flexible and welcoming to new arrivals.
The Tone of the Setting

The tone of Belavadös blends atmospheric fantasy, horror, and industrial decay with moments of resilience, discovery, humor, and humanity. The world is dangerous, but it is not hopeless. Players are encouraged to define what their characters protect, pursue, resist, or attempt to change within it.

Belavadös is a world of iron rails, rune-lit engines, fogbound ports, skyship harbors, bureaucratic institutions, and imprisoned gods whose existence still shapes daily life. Cities depend on infrastructure that is both industrial and arcane. Rail networks connect distant provinces. Ferries and skyships move goods and people across dangerous regions. Prisons beneath major cities contain weakened divine entities whose ichor powers medicine, alchemy, necromancy, industry, and political influence.
Civilization did not destroy its gods. It learned how to survive alongside what remained of them.

The setting treats logistics, travel, administration, and infrastructure as active parts of storytelling. Schedules matter. Ledgers matter. Small bureaucratic failures can become the first warning signs of something far worse.
The Ledger of Death

One of the most feared systems in the world is the Ledger of Death, governed beneath the cold gaze of the god Nefarokir. In Belavadös, every death is recorded with terrifying precision. Entire kingdoms depend upon those records remaining accurate.
When the ledger functions properly, society endures.
When it fails, reality begins to fracture.

The dead return to homes where they no longer belong. Names disappear from official records overnight. Families lose proof of their own existence. Graves open from within. Inheritance systems collapse. Entire bloodlines vanish because of clerical errors no living person remembers making.
And worst of all are those who try to escape their appointed death.
Nefarokir does not forgive stolen years.

Those hunted by the ledger rarely die cleanly. Coincidences become fatal patterns. Bridges collapse beneath a single pair of footsteps. Lamps burst. Horses panic. Knives slip. Bones snap. Eventually even skeptics understand the truth.
Nefarokir is correcting his ledger.
Soulbounds and Continuity

The world also contains rare individuals known as Soulbounds, people capable of accessing all Fifteen Arcane Disciplines rather than being tied to a single magical tradition. These individuals often experience fragmented memories and instincts from previous lives through a phenomenon known as Continuity.

Some become brilliant scholars, tacticians, healers, or protectors. Others destabilize under the strain of overlapping identities and converging magic. Governments and institutions quietly monitor Soulbounds while publicly minimizing their existence.
Campaign Structure

The campaign supports multiple scales of play. Some stories may involve larger adventuring parties, while others may focus on smaller groups or one-on-one narratives unfolding within the same shared timeline. Actions taken by one group may influence the broader world in measured and deliberate ways without forcing every storyline into a single path.
This structure allows different playstyles, schedules, and comfort levels to coexist naturally.

Sessions are hosted online using Foundry Virtual Tabletop through Molten Hosting. The campaign uses Dungeons & Dragons 5th Edition with custom character sheets, integrated homebrew systems, and optional homebrew races designed specifically for the setting’s cultures, history, and political structures. These options are meant to deepen immersion rather than overwhelm players, and no prior setting knowledge is expected.
New and Experienced Players Welcome
New players are absolutely welcome. There is no expectation of system mastery or extensive roleplay experience. Support will be available during onboarding, character creation, and play.
Experienced players will find evolving political landscapes, layered world systems, long-term consequences, and opportunities for meaningful character-driven storytelling.

Character creation includes a short alignment and perspective questionnaire designed to help integrate characters smoothly into the tone and moral complexity of the setting. It is not a test and does not restrict creativity. The goal is simply to help establish characters who feel grounded in the world and connected to its themes.
Table Culture and Development

The table culture is collaborative, patient, communicative, and welcoming. Respect for boundaries, player comfort, and shared storytelling are core priorities. Preparation is designed to support player agency and improvisation rather than force predetermined outcomes. The campaign evolves in response to player choices, interests, and discoveries.

Because the world is still actively developing, players joining early should expect some systems, mechanics, regions, and lore to evolve over time. Feedback is welcomed and appreciated, especially regarding pacing, accessibility, clarity, and overall experience.
The World Beneath the Rails

Belavadös is a setting shaped by ancient horror, industrial ambition, elemental magic, fractured history, and societies attempting to hold themselves together beneath the weight of things far older than they are.
For now, the world remains open.
The rails still run. The skyships still fly. And beneath the cities of Belavadös, the hungry gods wait.

1. The Crucible Wardens
armored relic-wardens and rail marshals
Doctrine and Operations
Location Network
Hierarchy and Roles
High Anvil: strategic commander and keeper of the sealed charter.
Reliquary Marshals: decide whether an item is studied, licensed, sealed, or broken.
Rail Paladins: armored escorts for relic convoys and ichor seizures.
Ink-Sparks: apprentice archivists who maintain witness logs and curse indices.
Mercy Factors: healers assigned to prevent containment from becoming cruelty.
DM Use and Quest Hooks

Use them when the party finds a god-made device, black-market ichor battery, unstable construct, cursed thundercoil, illegal portal key, or pre-rebellion divine prison component. They are helpful, intimidating, and convinced they know better than the public.
A Warden relic-car arrives sealed from the inside; the crew is alive, silent, and writing the same sentence in different hands.
A village wants the party to hide a healing engine before the Wardens confiscate it; the engine works only because it is fed pure ichor.
A chapter commander offers rail passes if the party recovers a stolen boiler-heart from a black-market skyship.
Faction Moves, Rewards, and Clock
2. The Obsidian Diadem
fallen war-dominion and oath-bound imperial court
Doctrine and Operations
Location Network
Hierarchy and Roles
Diadem Regent: masked sovereign whose legitimacy depends on victory rites.
Black Adjudicators: oath judges, duel witnesses, and executionary magistrates.
Night Cavalry: Aburata shock riders who patrol railheads and caravan roads.
Glass Cantors: Gwynis psychic officers trained to listen through dreams.
Ashbound Auxiliaries: conquered locals offered status in exchange for obedience.
DM Use and Quest Hooks

Use them as a terrifying order-with-purpose antagonist. They are not random tyrants; they keep trains punctual, streets lit, and monster incursions contained, then demand souls, secrets, and obedience as payment.
A Diadem court offers to restore a dead heir’s legal identity if the party erases a rebel name from Nefarokir’s records.
A black skyship descends with supplies after a disaster, then refuses to leave until the town signs an obedience charter.
A defecting Glass Cantor carries proof that the Diadem’s pure-ichor rites are awakening something beneath Sszaruun.
Faction Moves, Rewards, and Clock
3. The Choral Synod
many-peopled temple hegemony and pilgrim fleet
Doctrine and Operations
Location Network
Hierarchy and Roles
Cantor-Sovereigns: doctrinal rulers who claim to hear the final hymn.
Reliquary Captains: skyship, steamship, and submarine commanders guarding sacred cargo.
Choir-Castes: ranked faithful assigned to labor, song, guard duty, medicine, or war.
Doubt Inquisitors: polite investigators who diagnose heresy as spiritual illness.
Pilgrim Debtors: converts whose travel and medicine debts bind them to Synod service.
DM Use and Quest Hooks
Use them as alluring antagonists or uneasy allies. Their hymns genuinely heal, their processions protect roads, and their teachings also push entire settlements toward obedient ecstasy.
A Synod submarine returns from Thalryss with no crew, only a coral organ still singing in five voices.
A village cured by Synod medicine now dreams the same skyward staircase and begins dismantling its own rail station for holy materials.
A Doubt Inquisitor hires the party to investigate a heresy that may actually be the truth.
Faction Moves, Rewards, and Clock
4. The Brass Concordat
cross-provincial diplomatic council and covert writ network
Doctrine and Operations
Location Network
Hierarchy and Roles
Assembly of Lamps: formal council of voting provincial envoys.
Lantern Writs: elite agents empowered to act where treaty law cannot.
Quiet Clerks: records officers who decide which truths enter public history.
Harbor and Rail Attachés: transit inspectors embedded across ports and stations.
Mercy Delegates: visible diplomats sent after disasters, scandals, and massacres.
DM Use and Quest Hooks
Use them as the reasonable institution whose solutions may be ethical, compromised, or terrifyingly pragmatic. They make excellent patrons when the party needs legal cover or travel access.
A Lantern Writ asks the party to stop a war without leaving evidence the Concordat was involved.
A treaty ledger lists a settlement that nobody remembers building, yet rail tickets to it keep printing.
A public hearing about diluted ichor grades turns into a murder investigation when every witness forgets the same minute.
Faction Moves, Rewards, and Clock

death-ledger assassin cult and ritual contract office
Doctrine and Operations
Location Network
Hierarchy and Roles
Veil Listener: a prophetic contract-reader whose identity is never public.
Black Ledger Hands: senior assassins who accept or reject petitions.
Candle-Mutes: initiates who maintain shrines, poisons, disguises, and corpse routes.
Debt Saints: legendary killers whose names are invoked but rarely spoken aloud.
Unwritten Clients: nobles and officials who buy deaths, then deny the cult exists.
DM Use and Quest Hooks
Use them for horror, moral choice, and bureaucracy-as-terror. The cult is not merely evil; it can expose hidden crimes, punish tyrants, and still be a nightmare of sanctified murder.
A contract names someone who died three years ago, yet their body keeps appearing at rail stations.
The party is hired to protect a target whose death would actually repair a dangerous breach in Nefarokir’s records.
A Candle-Mute defects with a prayer-book showing that one of the party’s allies was purchased long ago.

ichor-mutated swarm culture and wetland brood network

Use them for body horror, ecological tragedy, and enemy adaptation. The Myriad is not only a monster faction; it is what happens when industry poisons living water with divine residue.

rows: A disciplined, oath-bound order that believes civilization survives only when the most dangerous inventions are catalogued, sealed, licensed, or destroyed. Diluted ichor is permitted in emergency medicine, locomotive stabilization, rune batteries, and anti-curse sealants. Pure ichor is contraband unless locked under Warden seal; recovered pure ichor is often the first cause of moral failure inside the order.
