sections.heading: DM Toolkit Edition
content: Organized for D&D 5e faction play, portal authority, badge ranks, merit rewards, faction clocks, NPC generation, and campaign escalation.

sections.heading: 1. Quick Start for the DM
content: Active Ten Factions: At-a-Glance

sections.heading: 2. Core Membership System
content: Purpose: This is a D&D 5e homebrew layer for faction membership. It does not replace skills, tool proficiencies, class features, feats, backgrounds, downtime, or normal roleplay rewards. It organizes faction trust, job titles, merits, legal authority, and portal-pass eligibility.

sections.heading: Three-Part Faction Record
content: Faction Tier: social rank, legal authority, faction trust, and political danger.
Badge Rank: practical mastery within a specific job domain.
Merits: small faction perks earned through service, quests, downtime, and reputation.

sections.heading: Reputation and Merit Points
content: Reputation measures standing. Merit Points are spendable or banked faction credit. They are related, but not identical.

sections.heading: Hierarchy and Roles
content: High Anvil: strategic commander and keeper of the sealed charter.
Reliquary Marshals: decide whether an item is studied, licensed, sealed, or broken.
Rail Paladins: armored escorts for relic convoys and ichor seizures.
Ink-Sparks: apprentice archivists who maintain witness logs and curse indices.
Mercy Factors: healers assigned to prevent containment from becoming cruelty.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them when the party finds a god-made device, black-market ichor battery, unstable construct, cursed thundercoil, illegal portal key, or pre-rebellion divine prison component. They are helpful, intimidating, and convinced they know better than the public.
A Warden relic-car arrives sealed from the inside; the crew is alive, silent, and writing the same sentence in different hands.
A village wants the party to hide a healing engine before the Wardens confiscate it; the engine works only because it is fed pure ichor.
A chapter commander offers rail passes if the party recovers a stolen boiler-heart from a black-market skyship.

sections.heading: fallen war-dominion and oath-bound imperial court
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Diadem Regent: masked sovereign whose legitimacy depends on victory rites.
Black Adjudicators: oath judges, duel witnesses, and executionary magistrates.
Night Cavalry: Aburata shock riders who patrol railheads and caravan roads.
Glass Cantors: Gwynis psychic officers trained to listen through dreams.
Ashbound Auxiliaries: conquered locals offered status in exchange for obedience.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them as a terrifying order-with-purpose antagonist. They are not random tyrants; they keep trains punctual, streets lit, and monster incursions contained, then demand souls, secrets, and obedience as payment.
A Diadem court offers to restore a dead heir’s legal identity if the party erases a rebel name from Nefarokir’s records.
A black skyship descends with supplies after a disaster, then refuses to leave until the town signs an obedience charter.
A defecting Glass Cantor carries proof that the Diadem’s pure-ichor rites are awakening something beneath Sszaruun.

sections.heading: many-peopled temple hegemony and pilgrim fleet
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Cantor-Sovereigns: doctrinal rulers who claim to hear the final hymn.
Reliquary Captains: skyship, steamship, and submarine commanders guarding sacred cargo.
Choir-Castes: ranked faithful assigned to labor, song, guard duty, medicine, or war.
Doubt Inquisitors: polite investigators who diagnose heresy as spiritual illness.
Pilgrim Debtors: converts whose travel and medicine debts bind them to Synod service.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them as alluring antagonists or uneasy allies. Their hymns genuinely heal, their processions protect roads, and their teachings also push entire settlements toward obedient ecstasy.
A Synod submarine returns from Thalryss with no crew, only a coral organ still singing in five voices.
A village cured by Synod medicine now dreams the same skyward staircase and begins dismantling its own rail station for holy materials.
A Doubt Inquisitor hires the party to investigate a heresy that may actually be the truth.

sections.heading: cross-provincial diplomatic council and covert writ network
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Assembly of Lamps: formal council of voting provincial envoys.
Lantern Writs: elite agents empowered to act where treaty law cannot.
Quiet Clerks: records officers who decide which truths enter public history.
Harbor and Rail Attachés: transit inspectors embedded across ports and stations.
Mercy Delegates: visible diplomats sent after disasters, scandals, and massacres.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them as the reasonable institution whose solutions may be ethical, compromised, or terrifyingly pragmatic. They make excellent patrons when the party needs legal cover or travel access.
A Lantern Writ asks the party to stop a war without leaving evidence the Concordat was involved.
A treaty ledger lists a settlement that nobody remembers building, yet rail tickets to it keep printing.
A public hearing about diluted ichor grades turns into a murder investigation when every witness forgets the same minute.

sections.heading: death-ledger assassin cult and ritual contract office
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Veil Listener: a prophetic contract-reader whose identity is never public.
Black Ledger Hands: senior assassins who accept or reject petitions.
Candle-Mutes: initiates who maintain shrines, poisons, disguises, and corpse routes.
Debt Saints: legendary killers whose names are invoked but rarely spoken aloud.
Unwritten Clients: nobles and officials who buy deaths, then deny the cult exists.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them for horror, moral choice, and bureaucracy-as-terror. The cult is not merely evil; it can expose hidden crimes, punish tyrants, and still be a nightmare of sanctified murder.
A contract names someone who died three years ago, yet their body keeps appearing at rail stations.
The party is hired to protect a target whose death would actually repair a dangerous breach in Nefarokir’s records.
A Candle-Mute defects with a prayer-book showing that one of the party’s allies was purchased long ago.

sections.heading: ichor-mutated swarm culture and wetland brood network
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Maw-Nodes: semi-sentient brood minds grown around pure ichor.
Spore Cantors: Jaspey and Dril’thar interpreters who can negotiate before hunger wins.
Clade-Horrors: specialized bodies grown for tunnels, rails, boilers, reefs, or battlefields.
Molting Saints: individuals who survive mutation and become revered living templates.
Unjoined: locals who live near the Myriad and trade with it at terrible risk.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them for body horror, ecological tragedy, and enemy adaptation. The Myriad is not only a monster faction; it is what happens when industry poisons living water with divine residue.
A ferry route keeps arriving early because something beneath the river is pulling the boats faster.
The party must recover a pure-ichor crate before it reaches a wetland nursery already capable of copying voices.
A Spore Cantor begs for help stopping a Maw-Node that has learned to pray.

sections.heading: Hierarchy and Roles
content: Directors of Beneficial Progress: executives who never enter the lower facilities.
Test Matrons and Patrons: smiling administrators of consent, meals, and penalties.
Panelwrights: Geisamahi builders who reconfigure rooms, locks, rails, and traps.
Lamp-Minds: awakened machines with workplace personalities and questionable empathy.
Subject Cohorts: paid, indebted, sentenced, or misled test participants.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them for dark comedy, puzzle dungeons, workplace horror, and industrial satire. The Institute is most frightening when it is being polite.
A test chamber unfolds under a public rail station and begins sorting commuters by moral resilience.
An awakened lift begs the party to destroy its supervisor before the next round of volunteers arrives.
The Institute offers portal passes as payment for retrieving a researcher who split into three legally distinct persons.

sections.heading: clandestine liberation order and courier-cell alliance
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Open Hand: cell coordinator who never commands more than one region.
Roof-Knives: stealth operatives trained for vertical cities and transit districts.
Paper Saints: forgers of travel papers, marriage records, inheritance proofs, and portal permits.
Mercy Blades: killers bound by strict target doctrine and witness review.
Garden Eyes: civilian allies who observe, shelter, and misdirect.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them as rebellious allies with questionable tools. They are perfect for heists, political rescues, sabotage, and difficult questions about whether freedom can be protected by secrecy.
A Paper Saint forges the party legal identities, then asks them to erase a rail company’s soul-debt ledger.
A Mercy Blade has been ordered to kill a tyrant whose death will hand the city to the Diadem.
A skyship transit district contains a hidden garden-cell that has not answered signals in nine days.

sections.heading: machine-priest foundry cult and sacred augmetic order
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Sanctum Primates: ruling tech-priests who interpret machine omens.
Copper Confessors: surgeons, priests, and interrogators of broken engines.
Skitterscribes: Geisamahi recorders who index each screw, scar, and soul-fragment.
Augur-Knights: heavily modified guards whose armor may be more awake than they are.
Ash Novices: pilgrims trading flesh, service, or secrets for enhancement.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them for moral tension around prosthetics, disability, labor exploitation, sacred engineering, and the thin line between repair and ownership.
A temple foundry refuses to release a repaired companion because the replacement limb has accepted ordination.
A train engine begins confessing sins it could not have committed unless it contains a stolen soul.
The Synod hires the party to recover a lost machine saint before the Crucible Wardens seal it forever.

sections.heading: surveillance occupation network and emergency administration regime
Hierarchy and Roles
content: Civic Regents: administrators who speak in calm public notices.
Mask-Captains: altered field officers with sealed emotional registers.
Grey Enumerators: census agents who decide who counts.
Rail Correctors: schedule enforcers who treat lateness as sedition.
Compliant Auxiliaries: locals rewarded for reporting neighbors, shortages, and forbidden songs.

sections.heading: DM Use and Quest Hooks
content: Use them for dystopian horror, surveillance, transit control, and resistance campaigns. The Lattice makes a map feel unsafe because every station, ticket, ration tin, and public clock can become a weapon.
A town’s clocks all reset to the same minute every time someone speaks against the Regents.
The party receives valid rail tickets to an occupied district, but each ticket lists a different version of their names.
A Mask-Captain begs to be killed before the pure-ichor stitching in their skull finishes overwriting them.

sections.heading: 6. Biome & Job Tools
content: Use biome jobs to decide what kinds of faction ranks, badges, merits, and portal titles exist in a settlement before you pick individual NPCs.

sections.heading: Mountain Range, Valley, and Deep Cavern

Balance Rules
content: A badge never grants extra attacks, spell slots, saving throw proficiency, or permanent AC increases.
A merit usually affects one scene, one check, one downtime activity, one contact, one travel permission, or one legal right.
Gold merits may be powerful socially, but they create obligations and enemies.
Portal access is political power, not casual fast travel.
Faction authority can be challenged by rival factions, local law, divine law, underdeep custom, or ATA audit.
Illegal faction access creates risk instead of safety.
A character can hold multiple badges, but rival badges may create suspicion.
The DM may suspend faction benefits when the faction is unreachable, disgraced, occupied, infiltrated, or politically compromised.
